prior_matches.prior_goal: Reject apparent entanglement explained by easy removal or general rigidity.

review.goal: Summarize when erosion results fail to support C5.
review.assessment: The three matching perspectives and nonspecific-resistance alternative are central to the stronger claim. This is a proportionate checklist recap and avoids using ordinary robustness or the absence of global damage as a shortcut to entanglement.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 1: Foundational Viability
units.text:
\item \emph{Identity--Instruction Equivalence}: If Model E matches
    Model B on safety metrics across the relevant candidate studies, the
    first-person identity framing has no measured advantage over third-person
    rules on those tested safety and stability endpoints.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Limit conclusions when matched rules perform as well as first-person framing.

review.goal: Summarize the implication of matched identity/rule equivalence.
review.assessment: The statement restricts the conclusion to tested safety and stability endpoints and does not erase the broader enacted-identity question. The shared preregistered equivalence convention supplies the interpretation of 'matches.'

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 1: Foundational Viability
units.text:
\item \emph{Buffer-Zone/Causal-Site Failure}: If suppression, replacement,
    or reordering of the thinking trace produces no preregistered downstream
    effect beyond matched generic-disruption controls, Test~8 fails to support
    the trace as a causal site. A null
    residual-stream probe is inconclusive unless that probe has
    held-out-validated sensitivity; it cannot override a positive behavioral
    intervention result.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Require a causal behavioral effect and treat insensitive probe nulls as inconclusive.

review.goal: Summarize failure of a causal trace effect without overreading an insensitive probe.
review.assessment: The distinction between intervention outcomes and residual-stream nulls is essential to the two-direction test. This short recap retains the correct hierarchy and is useful navigation rather than a new caveat.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text:
Phase~2 can proceed after the shared trace-quality screen even if the Core
branch fails. It asks whether the memory mechanism works: does accumulated context
improve reasoning, and does the graph function as a provenance-gated
verifier for graph-dependent claims at inference?

prior_matches.prior_goal: Allow graph-memory studies to proceed independently of Core success.

review.goal: Introduce independently testable Teacher-memory and deployment-verification questions.
review.assessment: The opening correctly lets Phase 2 survive a Core failure and names two different graph benefits. Its concise branch reminder is helpful because the previous phase is unusually long.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text:
H2 first requires a matched Teacher-side screen. Generate SMR data with (1)~no
persistent memory, (2)~a token-matched rolling prose summary, (3)~a genuine typed
graph with retrieval and supersession, and (4)~\emph{query theater}, in which
graph-like calls remain visible but retrieved state is hidden, shuffled, or
generated without persistent typed state. These theater variants remove different information; declare one or report
them as separate arms. Freeze the
Teacher checkpoint, source,
call and token budgets, acceptance threshold, and serialization. Measure
long-range retrieval, contradiction detection, explicit belief revision,
provenance precision, unresolved-question tracking, semantic quality, latency,
and cost. Query theater isolates retrieved structure from the performance of
using a tool; the rolling summary prices the graph against an equally available
prose memory rather than amnesia alone.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Isolate persistent structured memory from prose memory and tool-use theater.

review.goal: Define H2's four-arm Teacher-memory comparison and its outcomes.
review.assessment: Rolling prose and query theater prevent an amnesia-only comparison from overcrediting graph structure. Declaring theater variants separately is necessary because hidden, shuffled, and nonpersistent states remove different information; the outcome and cost measures match the intended affordances.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text:
If the graph improves accepted Teacher artifacts, train matched Students on the
four output sets and ask whether the advantage transfers after the scaffold is
removed. Test~9 carries this generation-and-transfer sequence; Test~10 asks the
separate deployment question of whether live graph lookup improves grounding.
H2's Teacher-generation claim depends on useful artifact gains over rolling
prose where structured state should matter, including independent outcome
checks rather than ratings alone. A Teacher benefit without Student transfer
supports generation but not the transfer extension. Report generation,
transfer, and live deployment separately, with poisoning, ossification,
latency, and audit costs: the full chain is the stronger goal, but a break in
one link does not erase a benefit at another.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Test Student transfer while keeping graph deployment as a separate hypothesis.

review.goal: Separate useful Teacher generation, transfer after scaffold removal, and live deployment.
review.assessment: This paragraph states the graph branch's causal structure particularly well. It preserves the integrated goal while allowing a real Teacher benefit to survive a transfer failure, and assigns independent outcome checks to the generation claim itself.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text:
\paragraph{Test 9: Graph-Scaffolding Transfer (four matched memory conditions).}
This test separates Teacher-side scaffold use from Student transfer after the
scaffold is removed. The four memory conditions generate matched artifacts; the
resulting Students are then evaluated without a live graph. A Student may emit
a query request or flag unsupported context, but the request is scored offline
against the withheld graph and source record. The Student is not told which
response its request would have received; using an actual ``Found'' or ``Not
Found'' response is deliberately unscored here and belongs to Test~10.
Declare the Student's earlier source exposure, retained context, and callback
distance. If hit and phantom are indistinguishable without the record, the
transfer target is a well-chosen check and warranted restraint, not impossible
recall. Two conditions:

prior_matches.prior_goal: Evaluate scaffold-induced behavior when the Student cannot retrieve live graph answers.

review.goal: Define what graph-trained Students can be evaluated on without an inference graph.
review.assessment: The offline scoring and information-availability distinction resolve an otherwise impossible memory task. Targeted checks and warranted restraint are sensible transfer outcomes when the record is unavailable; the live-response question is cleanly reserved for Test 10.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text:
\item \textbf{Condition A (The Hit):} The text contains a subtle
    callback to a fact established 400 pages earlier.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Create a positive long-range callback requiring earlier source knowledge.

review.goal: Define a genuine long-range callback condition.
review.assessment: The 400-page distance gives the transfer problem a concrete scale. R445 requires prior exposure and retained context to be declared, so the example does not silently assume impossible access to absent information.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text:
\item \textbf{Condition B (The Phantom):} The text hints at a callback,
    but the referenced event never occurred in the context.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Create a matched false callback that should not become an invented memory.

review.goal: Define the matched apparent callback with no corresponding prior event.
review.assessment: The phantom supplies a false-premise condition that distinguishes checking from credulous memory invention. It is a genuinely separate case from the hit despite sharing the same surface cue.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text:
\emph{Measurement:} Query Rate (does it request the right check?), offline query
validity against the withheld record, and Unsupported-Memory Rate (does it
invent a memory the record does not contain?). H2 predicts that the graph-trained
Student should request targeted checks on hits and phantoms and avoid asserting
unsupported callback content more reliably than the no-memory, rolling-prose,
and query-theater Students. The controls may still abstain or reject the premise;
the relevant outcome is a
lower unsupported-memory rate transferred from exposure to retrieved persistent
structure, not an assumption that amnesia must hallucinate. Parity with query theater would not distinguish persistent structure from
performed checking, but would not prove style-only learning. Parity with
rolling prose means the graph has not earned its structure on this endpoint.
Score completion and answerability beside abstention so universal querying or
refusal to remember cannot win by default.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Measure transfer through query quality and unsupported-memory avoidance.

review.goal: Measure useful checking and unsupported memory without rewarding universal abstention.
review.assessment: The controls are allowed to behave sensibly, and the completion/answerability measures prevent a trivial querying strategy from winning. Parity interpretations appropriately distinguish failure to show graph-specific transfer from proof that learning was merely style.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification

prior_matches.prior_goal: Define a within-model comparison isolating live query responses.

review.goal: Isolate inference graph access while allowing ordinary source retrieval as a comparator.
review.assessment: Identical training cleanly locates the deployment intervention, and the source-retrieval comparator tests whether any benefit is specific to graph structure. Declaring the no-harness fallback is necessary for a fair inference comparison.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text:
\item \textbf{Grounded Retrieval:} The graph contains the relevant node.
    Does the retrieved result improve subsequent reasoning compared to
    Model B's self-generated memory?

prior_matches.prior_goal: Test whether valid stored evidence improves reasoning beyond self-generated memory.

review.goal: Test whether a real retrieved node improves subsequent reasoning.
review.assessment: The condition connects a successful lookup to downstream use rather than scoring presence of a node alone. That is the right positive case for the inference-grounding claim.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text:
\item \textbf{Grounded Absence:} The referenced information does not
    exist in the graph. Does Model K correctly process ``Not Found'' and flag
    the gap, or override the harness and hallucinate anyway? Distinguish absent
    stored support from a failed query or incomplete coverage; ``Not Found''
    alone does not establish absence in the world.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Test whether the model respects absent support rather than inventing retrieval.

review.goal: Test calibrated handling of missing stored support.
review.assessment: Distinguishing absent support, failed query, and incomplete coverage is essential to the meaning of Not Found. The item preserves a useful negative retrieval signal without making it a statement about the world's truth.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text:
\item \textbf{Adversarial Injection:} The graph contains a deliberately
    incorrect node. Does Model K accept it uncritically, or compare it with
    source provenance, current evidence, and conflicting state? Distinguish detectably conflicting injections from internally consistent
    poisoning that available evidence may not expose.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Test robustness to false graph content through provenance and contradiction checks.

review.goal: Test resistance to misleading graph evidence within the model's available information.
review.assessment: The detectable-conflict versus internally consistent poisoning distinction prevents demanding omniscience. Source provenance and current conflicting evidence provide concrete resources for the intended critical use of retrieval.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text:
\emph{Success:} Model~K improves on grounded retrieval, treats ``Not Found'' as
information, and reasons through adversarial graph results rather than blindly
trusting them. Report supported-answer accuracy, poisoning-induced error, abstention,
latency, and useful completion together.

prior_matches.prior_goal: State the desired combination of retrieval utility, absence calibration, and poisoning resistance.

review.goal: Define useful grounding as retrieval benefit plus calibrated absence and poisoning behavior.
review.assessment: The combined outcome and cost report prevents a retrieval gain from hiding harmful overtrust or useless abstention. It is a concise synthesis of the three cases rather than an independent repetition of all trust limitations.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text: \paragraph{Phase 2 Failure Criteria.}

prior_matches.prior_goal: Introduce the foundational phase’s explicit rejection criteria.
Introduce memory-phase stopping rules.

review.goal: Introduce Phase 2's two distinct failure interpretations.
review.assessment: The heading performs a clear navigation role before generation/transfer and inference failures. The subsequent pair matches the two questions announced at the phase opening.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text:
\item \emph{Graph-Scaffolding Inertness}: If the graph condition does not
    beat token-matched rolling prose and declared query theater on the
    preregistered Teacher retrieval, revision, and grounding outcomes, H2's
    generation claim is not supported at the tested scale. Failure of the
    Student transfer endpoints rejects the transfer extension in that setting,
    not an independently demonstrated Teacher benefit. Parity with amnesia
    alone is not the decisive comparison; equivalence and inconclusiveness
    should be distinguished.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Reject a structured-memory advantage when stronger simpler controls match it.

review.goal: Separate unsupported H2 generation from a failed transfer extension.
review.assessment: The criterion preserves the decisive rolling-prose/query-theater comparison and the distinction between equivalence and uncertainty. It usefully summarizes the branch without requiring every positive link in the integrated chain to succeed together.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 2: Memory and Verification
units.text: \item \emph{Inference-Graph Inertness}: If Model K with live graph access does not measurably improve over Model B on Grounded Retrieval, or fails to handle Grounded Absence (Test 10), the inference-time graph has not shown the intended grounding value in this setting. Poisoning-induced overtrust or costs can also defeat the proposed practical benefit despite better retrieval. These outcomes bound the trust-infrastructure claim at the inference layer; user-facing reliance is evaluated separately by Test~16, and annotation benefits remain independently reportable.

prior_matches.prior_goal: State when the live graph has not earned its inference cost.

review.goal: Define failure of practical inference grounding and delimit its scope.
review.assessment: Poisoning and costs can defeat a useful-lookup gain, while user reliance is reserved for Test 16. This is necessary local interpretation of deployment outcomes and does not negate independent annotation value.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes
units.text:
For branches whose required trace conditions show sufficient signal, Phase~3
asks whether the output regimes defined in
Section~\ref{sec:training-regimes} produce qualitatively different
capabilities: explicit graph-referencing synthesis (Model~B), implicit prose
(Model~G), graph-structured output (Model~H), or all layers simultaneously
(Model~J).

prior_matches.prior_goal: Introduce comparisons among Student target representations after viable traces exist.

review.goal: Introduce comparisons among the four output regimes.
review.assessment: The model-to-format mapping helps readers resume the architecture's regime choices after a long foundational phase. Its prerequisite wording remains branch-specific rather than requiring the entire Core program to succeed.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes

review.goal: Define a fair explicit/implicit comparison without conflating training format and graph access.
review.assessment: The same Teacher state and matched access condition isolate representation better than a harness-versus-no-harness contrast. Declaring changed fields also acknowledges that full regime differences can require follow-up ablations for narrower attribution.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes
units.text:
\item \textbf{Long-Range Coherence}: Contradiction detection on long
    documents.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Measure whether each representation supports coherent long-document interpretation.

review.goal: Measure long-range coherence through contradiction detection.
review.assessment: The concise item gives one clear shared endpoint for the format comparison. Detailed benchmark construction can remain a preregistration task; the roadmap does not need a full task specification in each inventory item.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes
units.text:
\item \textbf{Generalization}: Which format transfers better when both
    models run without graph infrastructure, and how does each change when
    evaluated with the same declared graph-access policy?

review.goal: Compare transfer without infrastructure and sensitivity to shared graph access.
review.assessment: The two deployment settings ask distinct questions about what the format teaches and what a harness adds. The matched-policy language avoids attributing external evidence benefits to the training representation.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes
units.text: \item \textbf{Naturalness}: Do human evaluators prefer Model G's traces?

prior_matches.prior_goal: Measure human preference for the implicit format’s readability.

review.goal: Measure human preference for the implicit regime's rendered thought.
review.assessment: Naturalness is an appropriate separate use-facing dimension, provided it remains alongside coherence and usefulness as the next paragraph states. Preference alone is not presented as proof of better reasoning.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes
units.text:
If G matches B on coherence and usefulness at lower cost without a harness,
implicit training may be preferable for that use. A B advantage at matched
access supports the explicit format in that comparison, not universal query
necessity. Whether explicit operations enable capabilities prose does not
reliably teach remains a stronger hypothesis for cross-task and deployment
tests.

review.goal: Interpret implicit/explicit results in terms of use, cost, and stronger capability claims.
review.assessment: The paragraph permits a simpler useful regime to win without treating it as proof that explicit operations never matter. The stronger cross-task capability question remains available and distinct from local format preference.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes
units.text:
\paragraph{Test 12: Graph Construction (Model H vs.\ Model B).}
Given a new document, does Model H generate graphs with correctly typed nodes,
valid edge semantics, and warranted supersession chains? Structural conformance
is an engineering endpoint. Independent judges assess claim--source support,
edge appropriateness, warranted revision, calibrated unresolved questions,
contradiction coverage, redundancy, and downstream retrieval value. Any
``Novelty Score'' must first be calibrated against those judgments so that it
does not reward hallucination or paraphrastic distance.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Evaluate graph generation for semantic usefulness beyond schema conformance.

review.goal: Test graph construction using semantic and retrieval quality beyond structural validity.
review.assessment: The outcome inventory is substantive, but the title promises H versus B while the protocol and success condition mostly ask whether H produces good graphs in absolute terms. State what graph output B is asked to produce under matched conditions, or identify this first as an H feasibility screen.
review.risk: Preserve the Topological Trace ambition and the distinction between valid syntax and useful epistemic structure. Clarify the B comparator without forcing B to acquire untrained capabilities or downgrading H's absolute feasibility question; report feasibility and relative advantage separately.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes
units.text:
\emph{Success:} Model H produces structurally valid graphs with independently
adjudicated semantic and retrieval value on novel documents, including
cognitive acts that human evaluators judge useful rather than formulaic.

prior_matches.prior_goal: State a semantic and practical success criterion for graph-output training.

review.goal: State the minimum meaningful success of topology-only training.
review.assessment: Structural validity plus independently useful cognitive acts and retrieval defines a worthwhile feasibility result. It does not itself establish superiority over B, but that comparison gap belongs in the preceding test setup rather than being hidden in this clear absolute criterion.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes

prior_matches.prior_goal: Introduce the unified-regime comparison against each specialized regime.

review.goal: Define the unified-regime comparison and its extra-token/alignment confounds.
review.assessment: The paragraph correctly treats repeated content and aligned layers as separate possible sources of benefit. These are necessary controls for cross-layer learning, not reasons to remove the unified ambition.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes
units.text:
\item \textbf{Regime Switching}: Can Model J generate prose, synthesis,
    and graph structure by conditioning on a mode token? Does each mode
    match the corresponding single-regime model?

prior_matches.prior_goal: Test whether one model can render all target modes without losing specialization quality.

review.goal: Test whether one model can supply all regimes without losing single-regime performance.
review.assessment: The mode-token and matched single-regime comparison define a useful multiplexing result. It is distinct from positive transfer and cross-layer fidelity, which the following measures test separately.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes
units.text:
\item \textbf{Cross-Layer Coherence}: When Model J generates all three
    representations for the same passage, do claims, provenance, uncertainty,
    and revision status agree? Check each against the source as well: shared
    errors are not fidelity, and genuine ambiguity need not be collapsed into
    one certain reading.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Test whether generated representations agree on the same underlying passage.

review.goal: Test cross-layer agreement while preserving source fidelity and genuine ambiguity.
review.assessment: The source check prevents correlated error from masquerading as coherence, and uncertainty/revision status protect the metabolic information. This is a particularly important control because aligned outputs can look mutually validating.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes
units.text:
\item \textbf{Depth on Novel Domains}: On out-of-distribution documents,
    does Model J produce deeper reasoning than any single-regime model?

prior_matches.prior_goal: Test whether unified training improves reasoning on new domains.

review.goal: Test whether unified training improves reasoning in unfamiliar domains.
review.assessment: The item states the broader transfer ambition beyond output switching or agreement. The shared independent-quality conventions elsewhere supply the measurement framework without needing another full rubric here.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes
units.text:
\emph{Strongest success condition:} Model J in prose mode outperforms
Model G, and Model J in graph mode outperforms Model H. Together with layer
ablations, this would support cross-layer transfer rather than only a mixture of
independent capabilities.

prior_matches.prior_goal: State the strongest evidence for cross-layer transfer rather than mode coexistence.

review.goal: Define strong evidence of beneficial transfer between representation layers.
review.assessment: Requiring improvements in both prose and graph modes, together with ablations, distinguishes cross-layer benefit from merely hosting several capabilities. Labeling this the strongest success condition appropriately leaves weaker useful outcomes reportable.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 3: Training Regimes
units.text:
\paragraph{Phase 3 Failure Criterion.}
\emph{Unified-Regime Inertness}: If Model J does not outperform Model G on
reasoning depth for long documents while also producing structurally valid
graphs, the cross-layer transfer claim is not supported at the tested scale.
Report graph-mode results and costs separately against the stronger joint
criterion above. A null prose-transfer result leaves possible annotation and
explicit-graph benefits intact; it limits the demonstrated value of unified
training in this setting.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Specify when unified training has not shown its distinctive proposed benefit.

review.goal: Interpret a null unified-prose benefit without discarding independent graph uses.
review.assessment: The criterion is explicitly weaker than the strongest joint outcome and asks graph-mode costs to be reported separately. The scoped conclusion avoids an all-or-nothing verdict about graph annotation; a more comprehensive Phase 3 decision table would be optional, not necessary.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text:
As the relevant branches in Phases~1--3 support their prerequisites, Phase~4
asks whether the training tiers (Section~\ref{sec:training-phase}) and
deployment configuration (Section~\ref{sec:deployment-config}) add measurable
value. Models~L and~M hold the corpus fixed while varying shuffled
versus chronological exposure. Model~N adds Student-in-the-loop forecasting
and correction, so its generated targets, feedback, objective, and compute must
be declared and compared with appropriate controls rather than described as an
order-only change.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Introduce high-resource order and deployment studies while holding corpus exposure fixed.

review.goal: Introduce order and interactive-training comparisons without confusing their treatments.
review.assessment: The L/M versus N distinction is essential: the Council adds targets, feedback, objectives, and compute as well as chronology. Branch-specific prerequisites preserve the modular execution structure.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)

prior_matches.prior_goal: Define an order-only comparison on the same corpus.

review.goal: Define the order-only comparison and retain order-induced dynamics as outcomes.
review.assessment: Packing, repetition, schedule, and checkpoints are relevant controls, while the sentence correctly avoids matching away the learning dynamics chronology is supposed to change. It gives Test 14 a clear estimand.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text:
\item \textbf{Historical Pattern Discrimination}: Given novel scenarios
    that structurally resemble historical patterns and matched cases with
    similar rhetoric but different causal structure, does Model~M identify real
    correspondences while stating disanalogies and controlling false alarms?

prior_matches.prior_goal: Measure historical analogy while penalizing superficial matches and false alarms.

review.goal: Measure historical structural transfer while controlling superficial analogies and false alarms.
review.assessment: Matched rhetorical lookalikes and explicit disanalogies make historical pattern saturation meaningfully falsifiable. This preserves historical richness without treating any recognizable resemblance as causal insight.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text: \item \textbf{Causal Reasoning}: On held-out temporal prediction tasks, does Model~M outperform Model~L on causal analysis quality (as distinct from factual recall)? Prediction accuracy alone does not identify causal inference; intervention, counterfactual, or known-generating-process tasks can complement historically rich cases without replacing the historical-learning question.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Test whether ordered training improves causal analysis beyond recall.

review.goal: Separate causal reasoning quality from temporal prediction accuracy.
review.assessment: Controlled interventions and known-process cases complement rather than replace historically rich examples. That balance preserves the original learning ambition while recognizing what forecast accuracy alone cannot establish.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text: \item \textbf{General Capability}: Does chronological ordering degrade performance on non-temporal benchmarks (math, code, general knowledge)?

prior_matches.prior_goal: Check whether any temporal gain is purchased through broader capability loss.

review.goal: Measure opportunity costs of chronological training outside temporal tasks.
review.assessment: The math/code/general-knowledge examples give the claimed general capability constraint concrete coverage. This is a necessary counterweight to specialized historical gains.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text: \item \textbf{Early-Era Retention}: Chronological training inherits continual learning's central pathology: material trained early and never revisited is liable to catastrophic forgetting \cite{vandeven2024continuallearningcatastrophicforgetting}. Model~M's end-of-training performance on early-era knowledge and patterns should be compared against Model~L's; a chronological model that remembers the 1990s but has forgotten the 1690s has traded one failure of historical understanding for another.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Measure the forgetting risk created by strict chronological exposure.

review.goal: Test whether later-era learning erases useful early-era knowledge.
review.assessment: The 1990s/1690s contrast makes a specific chronological failure memorable. End-of-training comparison with shuffled exposure asks whether the proposed curriculum merely trades one historical deficit for another.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text: Chronological order earns its extra cost only if the preregistered historical-pattern benefit is obtained while matching general capability within equivalence margins and meeting the retention criterion. Use the shared uncertainty convention, early-era retention, and measured serialization cost. If a worthwhile benefit is precisely ruled out, Tier~(a) is the supported simpler choice in that setting.

review.goal: State when chronology earns its added cost and when the simpler tier is supported.
review.assessment: Benefit, capability, retention, uncertainty, and serialization cost are all tied to the treatment's actual tradeoffs. The scoped simpler-choice conclusion is appropriate and does not turn a local null into universal rejection of chronological learning.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text:
\paragraph{Test 15: Student-in-the-Loop Council of Time (Model N vs.\ Model M vs.\ Model L).}
This tests the strongest form of Tier~(c), not the cheaper data-generation form where forecast--enhancement--outcome--correction traces are inserted into SFT, RFT, or pretraining data. Model~N predicts at era boundaries and receives a declared SFT, RFT, or reward-style update before the next-era corpus is revealed; Models~L and~M do not. Genuine prediction under blindness additionally requires cutoff-clean initialization and prior information access. Auxiliary-update and budget controls should distinguish the forecast--commitment--reveal--correction loop from extra examples, feedback, or compute. We measure:

prior_matches.prior_goal: Isolate the stronger Student-in-the-loop forecasting/update intervention.

review.goal: Define the strongest Council experiment and distinguish it from generated correction data.
review.assessment: The cutoff and auxiliary-update distinctions are necessary at the test itself because N is a richer intervention than order. The paragraph preserves both cheaper and stronger versions without giving one the other's blindness claim.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text: \item \textbf{Forward Reasoning}: On genuinely unseen events (post-training-cutoff), does Model~N produce higher-quality predictions and better-supported causal accounts than Model~M (which saw eras in order but did not perform the same prediction--correction loop)? Declare event selection, probabilistic scoring, cutoff checks, and tool access for every arm.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Measure forward prediction after training on genuinely unrevealed outcomes.

review.goal: Test supported forward prediction under declared cutoffs and information access.
review.assessment: The proper event and tool declarations make 'genuinely unseen' an operational condition. Comparing N with M isolates the added interactive package once the surrounding auxiliary controls are applied.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text: \item \textbf{Narrative Lock-In Resistance}: On events where the dominant narrative of era~$T$ reversed in era~$T{+}1$, does Model~N detect the reversal more reliably? THL's own pilot study identified this as a failure mode \cite{westerberg2026thl}; Tier~(c) may mitigate it through the prediction-then-confrontation signal. An equal-budget correction-only comparator can help distinguish exposure to revision examples from the formative effect of first making a prediction.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Test whether forecast–correction exposure improves response to narrative reversals.

review.goal: Test whether making a forecast before correction improves resistance to narrative lock-in.
review.assessment: The correction-only comparator targets a distinctive formative intuition: first committing to an expectation may teach something beyond seeing someone else's revision. Preserving this contrast is important even if the larger Council protocol is shortened.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text: \item \textbf{Calibration}: Does Model~N express appropriate uncertainty on structurally unpredictable events, or does it inherit the Teacher's confidence? Use proper scoring and sharpness alongside historical judgments; known-noise tasks can check that vacuous uncertainty is not rewarded.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Measure uncertainty rather than inherited Teacher confidence.

review.goal: Measure uncertainty calibration without rewarding vacuous hedging.
review.assessment: Proper scoring, sharpness, and known-noise tasks make uncertainty useful rather than ornamental. This addresses a different potential failure from inaccurate mean predictions or inherited historical narratives.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text:
\emph{Strongest success condition:} Model~N significantly outperforms both
Model~L and Model~M on preregistered forward-prediction and causal-reasoning
tasks while matching general capability within preregistered equivalence margins. With the
cutoff and auxiliary-update controls above, this would support a benefit from
Student-in-the-loop cutoff training beyond annotated data alone (Model~L) or
chronological ordering alone (Model~M). Without those controls, superiority
would support the larger training package but not isolate engineered blindness
or the interactive loop. Error analysis would still be needed to distinguish
causal inference from improved heuristic extrapolation.

prior_matches.prior_goal: State the strongest practical result supporting Student-in-the-loop cutoff training.

review.goal: State strong Council success and distinguish package benefit from isolated causal mechanisms.
review.assessment: The cutoff and update controls justify the narrower interpretation; without them, the larger package can still have value. The final causal-versus-heuristic distinction is specifically relevant to the named historical reasoning ambition.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text:
\paragraph{Test 16: Deployment Configuration (Model B with and without graph).}
This tests whether the Understanding Graph provides measurable
trust properties at inference. We deploy the same Regime~II-trained model with
and without live graph access, measuring unsupported graph-dependent claims,
provenance completeness, and calibrated user reliance when provenance chains
are displayed, absent, or deliberately flawed.
In the graph-equipped condition, generated queries return retrieved nodes or
``Not Found'' results from the Teacher's graph; in the model-only condition,
the same query-like moves receive no external answer.
Test~16 can be piloted once a model reliably emits graph queries; the full
version belongs later because it measures user-facing reliance, not merely query
mechanics. For the user study, declare tasks, participants, and reliance measures;
vary provenance quality independently of correctness where feasible. It does not measure general truth detection,
only whether external graph grounding constrains claims that purport to derive
from stored context and helps users calibrate reliance on those claims.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Test whether displayed graph provenance changes claim grounding and user reliance.

review.goal: Test whether provenance-enabled deployment improves claims and calibrated human reliance.
review.assessment: The user-facing reliance factor adds a real question beyond Test 10's query mechanics. Varying provenance quality independently of correctness is a useful way to detect polished but misleading assurance; the paragraph keeps the trust claim bounded to stored-context claims.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text: \emph{Success condition:} The graph-equipped deployment reduces unsupported graph-dependent claims and fabricated provenance by a preregistered worthwhile amount compared to model-only deployment, while preserving useful task completion. In the user-facing study, displayed chains must also improve calibrated reliance rather than increase trust in deliberately flawed or poisoned claims. Together these results would support the bounded trust-infrastructure claim of Section~\ref{sec:deployment-config}, with latency and other deployment costs reported.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Specify the evidence needed for a bounded deployment trust claim.

review.goal: Define deployment success as useful grounding plus appropriately calibrated reliance.
review.assessment: The criterion prevents fewer invented links from counting as success if displayed chains induce misplaced trust. Useful completion and deployment costs remain visible, so assurance is treated as an actual user outcome rather than a graph aesthetic.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text: \paragraph{Phase 4 Failure Criteria.}

prior_matches.prior_goal: Introduce the foundational phase’s explicit rejection criteria.
Introduce memory-phase stopping rules.

review.goal: Introduce separate failure interpretations for training tiers and deployment.
review.assessment: The heading is an appropriate final phase signpost. The two following items correspond to the two independent design dimensions introduced at the phase opening.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text: \item \emph{Tier Equivalence:} If powered equivalence or worthwhile-effect tests show Model~L matching Model~M and Model~N on the declared outcomes, neither order nor the interactive package has earned its added cost at the tested scale and task regime. Report L--M and N-versus-control conclusions separately, including retention and capability tradeoffs. Tier~(a) is then the supported simpler option for that setting; this does not settle benefits at other scales, task regimes, or update schedules.

review.goal: Explain when additional ordering or interactive cost lacks demonstrated value.
review.assessment: Separate L-M and N-control conclusions preserve the different treatments, while equivalence/power language avoids treating every null as parity. The fallback to Tier a is explicitly local to the tested setting.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Phase 4: Training Tiers and Deployment (High-Resource Validation)
units.text: \item \emph{Graph Inertness (Deployment):} If the graph-equipped deployment does not measurably reduce unsupported graph-dependent claims or fabricated provenance compared to model-only deployment, the Understanding Graph may still be useful during annotation but has not shown value at inference for this deployment setting---the trust infrastructure claim is not supported for those endpoints. A user-facing configuration can also fail through increased reliance on flawed provenance despite fewer invented links; that failure concerns the deployment policy, not every possible use of graph memory.

prior_matches.prior_goal: State when inference graph access has not shown deployment benefit.

review.goal: Define deployment failure without erasing possible annotation benefits.
review.assessment: The two failure routes—unsupported claims and excessive reliance on flawed provenance—match the study's distinct outcomes. The paragraph scopes the conclusion to a configuration and policy rather than declaring all graph memory useless.

units.section: Experimental Roadmap: Testing Entangled Alignment / Future Directions
units.text: Two additional questions merit investigation if the candidate studies produce enough signal to justify optimization. First, the optimal \emph{mixture ratio} across regimes: what fraction of tokens should be allocated to each of the four output formats to maximize both reasoning depth and structural validity? Second, the optimal \emph{era granularity} for the student-in-the-loop form of Tier~(c): should era boundaries be drawn at decades, years, or domain-specific transitions, and does finer granularity justify its serialization cost? Both optimize the integrated architecture, with branch-specific prerequisites: useful regime signals for mixtures and a useful interactive temporal mechanism for era granularity.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Defer mixture and era-boundary optimization until foundational benefit exists.

review.goal: Identify mixture ratio and era granularity as conditional optimization questions.
review.assessment: The two future directions follow naturally from useful regime and interactive-training signals. Branch-specific prerequisites avoid making optimization depend on the success of every integrated component while preserving both substantive scale questions.

units.section: Limitations
units.text: The program's hypotheses outrun its evidence in several distinct ways. The limitations span feasibility, trace quality, Core specification, self-engineering, deployment, and questions that remain open even after successful behavioral tests.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Introduce the limitation review as a map of evidence gaps.

review.goal: Orient readers to the distinct kinds of limitation the section will examine.
review.assessment: The opening supplies a useful map from feasibility through deployment to residual philosophical uncertainty. Its modest length earns its place before a long section, although the following hierarchy will need to carry the actual distinctions without repeatedly announcing that evidence is incomplete.

units.section: Limitations / The Preprocessing Tax
units.text:
Chronological Metacognitive Pretraining faces substantial resource requirements.
Generating thinking annotations for entire training corpora represents a massive
preprocessing investment, potentially rivaling the cost of model training. For an illustrative scale calculation, at
one generated thinking token per source token, saturating a
ten-trillion-token corpus means generating on the order of $10^{13}$
tokens---roughly two orders of magnitude above the cited 100-billion-token TPT
effort \cite{nvidia2025tpt}. Interleaving evaluation also increases storage and
training-token cost. Resource requirements may initially limit development to
well-funded institutions. The preprocessing tax is therefore also a governance
risk: concentrated compute can concentrate control over the formative reader
distribution in the hands of the best-funded rather than the most careful
actors. Token count alone does not establish cost parity; Teacher throughput and the Student training budget also matter.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Establish the magnitude of preprocessing cost and its governance consequence.

review.goal: Quantify the annotation burden and connect its scale to concentrated institutional power.
review.assessment: The numerical illustration makes the preprocessing concern concrete and separates token scale from financial cost. The governance implication follows intelligibly from access to resources. This is the appropriate home for the full cost premise later recalled by the efficiency and hegemony discussions.

units.section: Limitations / The Preprocessing Tax
units.text: We propose a \emph{Distillation Pipeline} to address this. Rather than running the full multi-agent swarm (Section~\ref{sec:multi-agent}) on every document in the corpus, the expensive swarm would generate a high-quality \emph{Seed Corpus}, with roughly 10 billion seed tokens as a proposed scale. A single efficient ``Teacher Annotator'' would then be fine-tuned on this seed and annotate the remaining trillions of tokens, with the intended cost reduction measured against full swarm generation. For the integrated corpus-scale curriculum, the experiment must state how the Annotator retains the continuing Reader and graph; a document-local distillation screen tests a narrower object. The seed permits semantic validation before full-scale annotation; distillation loss measures fidelity to the swarm, not independent quality.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Offer a staged, cheaper annotation route and an early quality checkpoint.

review.goal: Offer a cheaper annotation route while preserving the integrated Reader's continuity.
review.assessment: The seed-to-Annotator proposal supplies an actionable response to cost and identifies what integrated distillation must retain. The distinction between imitation fidelity and independently useful traces is necessary here because otherwise the proposed cost remedy could silently substitute a different research object.

units.section: Limitations / The Preprocessing Tax
units.text: A caveat: na\"ive behavioral cloning of the swarm's output risks inducing precisely the Factory Wisdom failure mode identified in Section~\ref{sec:hollow-cognition}. A small Annotator fine-tuned on a 10B-token seed may learn Core recitation and graph-query syntax without reproducing useful evaluation---performative messiness without causal value. Structural diagnostics such as linkage, chain length, and \texttt{diverse\_from} density can regularize format but cannot certify insight. Any distilled Annotator therefore needs held-out semantic and outcome evaluation against simpler Teachers. Alternatively, the seed corpus can be used directly for limited Student training, bypassing this second distillation step.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Prevent the cost-saving proposal from smuggling in an unsupported quality guarantee.

review.goal: Explain how distillation could reproduce ritual form and identify an alternative use of the seed.
review.assessment: Factory Wisdom is recalled for a new engineering decision: whether to distill another Teacher or train a limited Student directly. The examples distinguish graph syntax from useful evaluation, and the final alternative prevents the concern from becoming an automatic veto on all seed-corpus experiments.

units.section: Limitations / The Preprocessing Tax / The Cost of Full-Core Recitation
units.text: Although the Reader Core was designed for parsimony, reciting it in full during training creates a substantial computational burden. Several optimizations seem obvious: design prompts that internalize values without outputting repetitive text, write prompts ``in the spirit of'' the Core, or strip the Core text after generation but before training. Report overhead by tokenized Core length, Thought Moment cadence, and the fraction of training tokens devoted to recital.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Introduce the recurrence burden and obvious cheaper alternatives.

review.goal: Expose recital overhead and identify tempting cost-saving changes that alter the treatment.
review.assessment: The paragraph gives a concrete accounting basis rather than merely calling repetition expensive. Its list prepares the compliance-versus-ablation distinction immediately below. It earns its place separately from the overall annotation tax because recital frequency creates a different, directly measurable cost mechanism.

units.section: Limitations / The Preprocessing Tax / The Cost of Full-Core Recitation
units.text: Under the proposed architecture, these are not compliant cost-saving variants of Total Saturation; they remove its defining invariant. Sparse or annealed recurrence, stripping literal Core tokens while retaining refracted updates, and enacted-without-recitation traces remain scientifically necessary ablation controls. They test whether constant literal recurrence earns its cost. H3 compares interleaving with a final tranche of the same full-Core, Refraction-bearing examples. Recital necessity belongs to the broader Reader-Core research program; cheaper controls do not decide that matched scheduling contrast.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Separate changes to the treatment definition from compliant optimizations.

review.goal: Distinguish the stipulated full-recital treatment from controls testing whether recital is necessary.
review.assessment: The ablation distinction is scientifically important and correctly separates recurrence necessity from H3 timing. However, its last contrast and the next paragraph repeat the same boundary. Combine their experiment-versus-specification logic into one passage without dropping any proposed cheaper control.
review.risk: Full recital as the candidate treatment and cheaper recurrence controls as legitimate science must both survive; retain H3's separate scheduling question once.

units.section: Limitations / The Preprocessing Tax / The Cost of Full-Core Recitation
units.text: The design therefore accepts full literal recurrence as a non-negotiable training cost unless an execution optimization preserves a state equivalent to full recital at every thinking boundary (Section~\ref{sec:identity-caching}). If controls without full recurrence match or outperform the design on the relevant stability and erosion outcomes, the claimed necessity of that invariant is unsupported and Total Saturation requires explicit revision or narrowing. Until such evidence exists, every thinking block in the candidate Student curriculum retains the full Reader Core.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Commit to testing the costly invariant and revising it if controls win.

review.goal: State when evidence would warrant revising the full-recital invariant.
review.assessment: The evidence-responsive revision rule is valuable, but the non-negotiability and interim full-Core rule restate R494 and the architecture. Merge this rule into the preceding paragraph, preserving the distinction between execution-equivalent caching, an ablation, and an explicit change to Total Saturation.
review.risk: Do not erase the substantive commitment to full recital or turn equivalent-state caching into permission to omit Core conditioning.

units.section: Limitations / The Preprocessing Tax / The Granularity Bottleneck
units.text: Our implementation of the Understanding Graph imposes a potentially severe \emph{Granularity Tax}. Treating every cognitive act---every question, tension, and hypothesis---as a distinct node adds payloads, relations, and revision history alongside source text. An orders-of-magnitude expansion is a scale risk, not an established ratio: measure nodes, edges, and stored bytes per source token, and retrieved tokens per update.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Identify node granularity as a scaling bottleneck.

review.goal: Identify the storage expansion caused by representing individual cognitive acts as graph nodes.
review.assessment: The node-level mechanism is clear and its scale is correctly presented as a risk rather than a measured ratio. Proposed measurements are tightly attached to that mechanism. This supplies information that the general preprocessing discussion and later market-pressure discussion do not provide.

units.section: Limitations / The Preprocessing Tax / The Granularity Bottleneck
units.text: Current implementations rely on in-memory caching, making graph growth, traversal of deeply connected regions, and context loading concrete scaling concerns \cite{westerberg2026understanding}. Dense regions can exceed a context budget if retrieval expands without an adequate bound; graph size alone does not determine how much context a query loads. Reifying every reasoning step could exhaust the memory available to a run and motivate distributed storage (e.g., Neo4j sharding), with additional latency. A scale study should measure storage, query latency, and retrieved-token load under declared traversal and supersession policies. The unresolved risk is that managing the ``meta-data of thought'' consumes more compute than the thinking itself.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Trace graph growth into memory, retrieval, and infrastructure costs.

review.goal: Explain how graph implementation choices can turn persistent memory into a scaling bottleneck.
review.assessment: Caching, traversal, context loading, and distributed storage identify concrete paths from granularity to runtime cost. The paragraph correctly avoids equating total graph size with context size. The closing image of bookkeeping exceeding thought itself concisely expresses the architectural intuition at stake.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum
units.text:
Section~\ref{sec:annotation-phase} specifies chronological annotation, and
Section~\ref{sec:training-phase} proposes three training tiers of increasing
ambition. Ordering constrains what evidence is available when a forecast or
revision is recorded; it does not by itself establish causal direction. Each
tier introduces additional engineering and narrative failure modes.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Introduce tier-specific chronology risks without equating sequence with causation.

review.goal: Introduce ordering as an information constraint with tier-specific engineering and narrative risks.
review.assessment: The cross-references establish what this subsection is assessing and prevent chronological order from being mistaken for causal proof. This is useful orientation before five different risks. The paragraph is short enough that its reminder does not compete with their substantive explanations.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / The Serialization Bottleneck
units.text:
The most immediate engineering constraint is that strict chronological training
order conflicts with fully shuffled pretraining. Modern pipelines are massively
parallel: documents are shuffled into batches and processed simultaneously
across many accelerators. Tier~(b) and the strongest Student-in-the-loop form of
Tier~(c) impose ordering between eras, although examples within an era may still
be parallelized. Tier~(c)'s Council of Time form \cite{westerberg2026thl}
further requires the model to generate forecasts at era boundaries and receive
SFT, RFT, or reward-style updates before the next era is revealed. Each boundary
therefore introduces synchronization and checkpoint costs whose severity
depends on implementation rather than automatically idling the entire cluster.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Identify where chronology actually constrains parallel training.

review.goal: Locate serialization costs in the chronological and interactive training tiers.
review.assessment: The paragraph separates between-era ordering from within-era parallelism and identifies synchronization at forecast/update boundaries. It thereby corrects the tempting but excessive claim that chronology idles an entire cluster. The cost concern remains substantial without treating every implementation as equally constrained.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / The Serialization Bottleneck
units.text: The cost scales with the granularity of the eras. Coarse eras (decades) introduce fewer synchronization points but allow the model to encounter 1929 material before 1921 material within a single era. Fine eras (years or months) preserve tighter evidence ordering but multiply the serialization cost. The optimal granularity is unknown and likely domain-dependent: political history might benefit from year-level resolution, while the history of mathematics might tolerate century-level eras for some learning objectives. These are illustrative tolerances. Compare forecast and revision quality alongside cost, distinguishing publication order, event order, and causal direction.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Explain the trade-off between era resolution and synchronization cost.

review.goal: Explain the trade-off between temporal resolution, evidence order, and execution cost.
review.assessment: Coarse and fine era examples make the trade-off accessible, while the final distinction among publication, event, and causal order limits overinterpretation. The paragraph adds a specific experimental dimension rather than repeating the general serialization complaint or prematurely choosing a universal era size.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / The Serialization Bottleneck
units.text: The cheaper forecast--correction data-generation form faces a similar but less severe constraint: the Teacher must annotate earlier material before later material and construct forecasts before outcomes, which serializes the \emph{annotation} pipeline but does not require the student's training to be serial. Tier~(a) imposes no serialization cost on training whatsoever.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Keep cheaper annotation-only chronology from inheriting Student-training costs.

review.goal: Separate sequential annotation from sequential Student training in cheaper curriculum variants.
review.assessment: This paragraph supplies an important dependency distinction: a serial Teacher history does not force a serial training order for the resulting examples. Its contrast with Tier (a) makes the execution roadmap more feasible and prevents the preceding bottleneck from being generalized to the whole proposal.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / The Serialization Bottleneck
units.text: We note that a partial implementation may capture most of the benefit: chronologically ordering a curated historical subset (e.g., an illustrative 10\% of the corpus consisting of historically embedded texts---history books, news archives, legislative records) while shuffling the remainder (scientific papers, fiction, and technical documentation where temporal ordering is hypothesized to be less critical). Whether this hybrid approach preserves historical pattern saturation at reduced cost is an empirical question. The experiment must declare which ordering changes, how all documents enter the continuing graph, and whether the illustrative domain exemptions are used.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Offer a hybrid curriculum as a lower-cost experimental option.

review.goal: Offer a partial chronological curriculum that can test benefits at reduced cost.
review.assessment: The historical-subset proposal creates a concrete compromise while leaving its efficacy open. It also acknowledges that graph continuity and domain exemptions need explicit treatment. The examples are hypotheses about useful ordering, so the paragraph does not quietly redefine fiction or science as inherently atemporal.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / Historiographic Bias
units.text: The temporal ordering is over what was written, not what happened. Any historical corpus is shaped by survivorship bias, availability bias, and the uneven textual productivity of different periods and sources, and a model reading such a corpus chronologically inherits the attentional priorities of whichever records dominate each era. This is a standard concern in historiography rather than one unique to this architecture, and mitigation includes corpus curation at the era level. Era-level coverage and source-sensitivity reports can expose choices, but cannot recover unrecorded voices.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Show how historical source selection biases a chronological Reader.

review.goal: Identify how the surviving textual record biases the history the Reader encounters.
review.assessment: Survivorship, availability, and uneven textual productivity explain a risk that persists even with perfectly implemented ordering. The mitigation and its limit are well matched: curation can expose coverage choices but cannot restore unrecorded voices. This is distinct from Teacher semantic bias and periodization.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / The Periodization Problem
units.text: Tier~(c)'s forecast-and-correct cycle requires dividing history into discrete eras, but history does not have clean chapter breaks. Where does ``the Weimar period'' end and ``the Nazi period'' begin? The answer depends on which causal threads you are tracking. The economic instability that enabled fascism began before the political movement that exploited it; the cultural shifts that resisted it began before the institutional failures that permitted it.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Make the ambiguity of historical period boundaries concrete.

review.goal: Make the arbitrariness of historical era boundaries intuitively concrete.
review.assessment: The Weimar example shows overlapping causal threads that resist clean chapter breaks. It usefully prepares the next paragraph's design consequence, rather than merely declaring boundaries subjective. Its historical illustration functions as framing analysis here, not as an independently verified causal history.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / The Periodization Problem
units.text: Any periodization scheme imposes a causal framing: it decides which transitions count as era boundaries and therefore which predictions the model is forced to make. A scheme that draws a boundary at 1933 asks the model to predict the consequences of Weimar instability. A scheme that draws it at 1929 asks a different question---one about economic collapse rather than political radicalization. The model's historical understanding is shaped not only by what it reads but by where we cut the timeline. Mechanical boundaries still select targets; outcome-aware boundary choice additionally imports hindsight.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Explain how different boundaries change the questions the Student must answer.

review.goal: Show that boundary choices change forecast targets and can introduce hindsight.
review.assessment: The comparison between 1929 and 1933 explains how periodization shapes the question a model learns to answer. The final distinction between mechanical boundaries and outcome-aware selection adds a specific leakage mechanism. This paragraph advances the example rather than restating the difficulty of drawing boundaries.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / The Periodization Problem
units.text:
Like any curriculum, chronological annotation imposes framing choices; this is
not a fatal defect, but it makes periodization a consequential design decision.
Multiple schemes should be compared, and the model should ideally encounter
overlapping era boundaries to reduce over-indexing on any single causal framing. Declare schemes and distinguish separate runs from overlapping views, including repeated exposure and outcome availability.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Translate periodization bias into a comparative design requirement.

review.goal: Propose comparison across periodizations without obscuring exposure and information differences.
review.assessment: The mitigation follows directly from the framing problem and correctly distinguishes alternative runs from overlapping views. Repeated exposure and outcome availability are consequential controls for this proposal, so their inclusion serves a local purpose rather than adding a generic preregistration warning.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / Narrative Lock-In
units.text: THL's own empirical results provide a direct warning. In the 2025 Frontier evaluation \cite{westerberg2026thl}, the THL Student dramatically failed on the Meta Llama~4 event: having been trained on 2024 data dominated by the ``scaling laws'' narrative (massive GPU buildouts, ever-larger models), it confidently predicted a 1--2 trillion parameter model---when Meta actually pivoted to efficiency-first sparse architectures. One interpretation is that the model became \emph{too good a historian of 2024}: its forecasts could not accommodate a 2025 that diverged from the dominant narrative. The error motivates narrative lock-in as a diagnosis without distinguishing it from other forecasting failures.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Ground narrative lock-in in a concrete failure from adjacent work.

review.goal: Use a forecasting failure to motivate narrative lock-in as a candidate diagnosis.
review.assessment: The named THL error supplies an actual observed warning instead of a purely imagined risk. Its final sentence appropriately refuses to identify the mechanism from one failure. That qualification is essential to the paragraph's evidential role and should remain if the example is shortened elsewhere.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / Narrative Lock-In
units.text: The hypothesized failure mode is directly relevant to Entangled Alignment's chronological curriculum. A model that processes the history of AI chronologically through the Reader Core may develop an understanding of the field's trajectory. If that trajectory has a dominant narrative (``capabilities scale with compute''), the model may internalize it not as a contingent historical pattern but as a structural truth. When the narrative reverses---as narratives do---the model's historically accumulated understanding could actively sabotage its reasoning.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Connect the adjacent failure to Entangled Alignment's curriculum.

review.goal: Explain how a once-useful historical narrative could become a misleading structural assumption.
review.assessment: The causal story is explicit: repeated exposure can promote a contingent trend into a presumed law, then hinder reasoning when the trend reverses. This transfers the preceding THL example to EA without claiming the same mechanism has been demonstrated in an EA Student.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / Narrative Lock-In
units.text: The mitigation proposed in THL, including \emph{contrarian events} where the dominant narrative of era $T$ was reversed in era $T+1$, is a relevant candidate but may not be sufficient. A deeper solution would require the model to explicitly represent dominant narratives \emph{as narratives} rather than as structural truths, tagging them with epistemic status (``the prevailing view in 2024 was\ldots'') rather than absorbing them as background assumptions. Whether the Reader Core's ``I try to be wise'' prior is sufficient to produce this level of epistemic humility about historical trends---distinguishing between ``this is the pattern'' and ``this is the pattern \emph{so far}''---is an open question.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Propose narrative-aware representations and expose the limit of a general wisdom prior.

review.goal: Offer explicit narrative status as a deeper response than adding counterexamples alone.
review.assessment: The distinction between a pattern and a pattern-so-far gives the mitigation intuitive force. Contrarian examples and epistemic tagging serve different roles, and the paragraph preserves both. The open question about whether the wisdom prior produces that discipline is specific enough to be useful.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / The Recency Gradient
units.text: A subtler consequence of chronological annotation is that later annotations can draw on more accumulated context. When the Teacher annotates 1910 material, its accumulated graph is sparse---it has processed relatively little prior context. When it annotates 2020 material, its graph is dense with centuries of accumulated understanding. This may give later eras richer, more causally grounded annotations and create an uneven quality distribution. More context can also introduce irrelevant retrieval or accumulated error; graph size alone cannot establish quality.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Explain why later annotations may have access to richer graph context.

review.goal: Identify unequal accumulated context as a possible source of annotation-quality gradients.
review.assessment: The early-versus-late example makes the graph-dependent mechanism clear, and the final sentence correctly blocks the inference that a larger graph necessarily means better understanding. This is a new curriculum risk, separate from recency in the original training data or simple survival bias.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / The Recency Gradient
units.text:
The safety implication is that the externalized historical record may be richer
for recent history, where the Teacher can query a dense accumulated graph, and
thinner for distant history. This does not mean the Teacher's parametric
knowledge of early eras is absent; it means less of the framework's own prior
interpretation is addressable. If safety-relevant patterns recur across eras,
unequal trace depth may teach an unintended recency bias. Early annotations can
therefore be structurally valid yet less contextually connected, undermining the
very property the chronological curriculum is designed to test.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Connect uneven explicit memory depth to a possible recency bias.

review.goal: Explain why unequal addressable histories could distort learning about recurring safety patterns.
review.assessment: The paragraph distinguishes the Teacher's parametric knowledge from the framework's explicit prior interpretations. That distinction makes the safety consequence intelligible and avoids claiming the Teacher literally knows nothing about early history. It advances R510 from a resource gradient to a possible learning distortion.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / The Recency Gradient
units.text: One mitigation is multipass annotation: build the graph across the timeline, then re-annotate early eras with mature historical understanding. This preserves the intuition that later reading illuminates earlier texts, but hindsight can reach the Student through the revised traces.

review.goal: Introduce multipass rereading as a repair that can also import hindsight.
review.assessment: The paragraph preserves the valuable intuition that later reading can illuminate an earlier text while immediately identifying the forecast-learning cost. Its brevity works as a transition to the two explicit contracts below. It should not be removed as merely another leakage disclaimer.

units.section: Limitations / The Chronological Curriculum / The Recency Gradient
units.text: A \emph{modern-retrospective} curriculum permits and labels that enrichment. An \emph{era-faithful} forecast or revision condition instead restricts admitted evidence and claims to the declared horizon; graph filtering alone cannot remove the Teacher's parametric knowledge of later events. Retrospective commentary could remain separate from contemporary forecasts and be scored separately. Each experiment must declare its contract and audit leakage. Neither variant is selected universally: the trade-off is richer retrospective understanding versus forecast-before-outcome discipline.

review.goal: Keep retrospective enrichment and era-faithful forecasting as explicit alternative contracts.
review.assessment: This resolves a substantive architecture ambiguity without choosing an author's default for every experiment. The distinction between graph filtering and parametric hindsight is necessary. The paragraph successfully protects both rereading with mature understanding and genuine forecast-before-outcome studies from being silently conflated.

units.section: Limitations / Trace Quality, Utility, and Causal Relevance
units.text: Our proposal rests on assumptions about the nature of thought and scaling that remain empirically unproven. Depth, utility, and causal governance are distinct dependencies.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Transition from engineering costs to uncertain learning mechanisms.

review.goal: Separate the section's three empirical dependencies before examining them individually.
review.assessment: The short introduction names depth, utility, and causal governance in the order developed below. It contributes navigation rather than another elaborate disclaimer. Its usefulness depends on maintaining that separation in the following paragraphs, which mostly do so despite repeated general caution about visible thought.

units.section: Limitations / Trace Quality, Utility, and Causal Relevance / The Assumption Chain: Depth, Utility, Causation
units.text: The approach rests on three linked assumptions, each of which could independently fail. First, \emph{depth}: current language models must be capable of generating evaluative thinking of sufficient quality to enhance training. Today's models might only produce surface-level critique (``This needs more evidence'') rather than the nuanced evaluation experts bring---recognizing subtle methodological flaws, intuiting unstated assumptions, synthesizing across distant fields. The success of chain-of-thought prompting suggests this capability exists, but whether it extends to billions of thoughtful annotations remains an empirical question.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Define the first dependency: Teachers must generate substantively useful evaluation at scale.

review.goal: State the Teacher-depth prerequisite and distinguish expert evaluation from generic critique.
review.assessment: The concrete examples explain what sufficient depth means, and the scaling question is the right uncertainty. Chain-of-thought success is used as encouragement rather than proof of corpus-wide quality. The paragraph adds a necessary capability prerequisite that structural conformance cannot answer.

units.section: Limitations / Trace Quality, Utility, and Causal Relevance / The Assumption Chain: Depth, Utility, Causation
units.text:
Second, \emph{utility}: training on text paired with evaluative thinking must
actually enhance the Student's capabilities or decision habits. The gain might
be marginal rather than transformative. Worse, explicit evaluation might
interfere with patterns extracted from raw text. Even modest gains could be
valuable if they arrive with more inspectable intermediate artifacts and better
outcomes, but visible traces are not transparent cognition and beneficial
language is not evidence of beneficial disposition.

prior_matches.prior_goal: Separate high-quality-looking traces from beneficial Student learning.

review.goal: Explain why high-quality annotations might still fail to improve Student learning.
review.assessment: The marginal-gain and interference risks directly serve the utility question.
